title: Medical Parasitology and Entomology
description: Laboratory diagnosis of blood, intestinal and tissue parasites, parasite morphology, and medically important arthropod vectors.

topics.title: Malaria Parasites: Morphology and Laboratory Diagnosis
topics.summary: Thick and thin films, species identification, parasite counting and RDTs.

notes.b: Microscopy of Giemsa-stained blood films remains the gold standard for malaria diagnosis in routine practice. The thick film (lysed red cells, more blood) is about 20–40 times more sensitive for detecting parasites; the thin film (fixed with methanol) allows species identification and morphology. Giemsa is used at pH 7.2 (Schüffner's dots and parasite features show best). A film is declared negative only after examining at least 100 high-power (oil immersion) fields of the thick film. Parasite density is counted against 200 white cells on the thick film (parasites/µL = parasites counted × WBC count ÷ 200, assuming 8,000 WBC/µL if not measured) or as % parasitised red cells on the thin film; > 5% (or > 250,000/µL) indicates hyperparasitaemia (severe malaria).
k: Thick film: sensitivity; thin film: species

notes.b: P. falciparum: small delicate rings, often multiple per cell and appliqué forms, crescent- or banana-shaped gametocytes, red cells not enlarged; mature trophozoites and schizonts are usually sequestered and rarely seen in peripheral blood (their presence indicates severe infection). P. vivax and P. ovale: enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots (ovale cells oval with fimbriated edges); amoeboid trophozoites in vivax. P. malariae: band-form trophozoites, 'rosette' schizonts with 6–12 merozoites, red cells normal or small. Rapid diagnostic tests detect parasite antigens: HRP2 (P. falciparum-specific, persists for weeks after treatment, may be missed with pfhrp2/3 gene deletions) and pLDH (pan-species or species-specific, clears faster). Quality control of slides and RDTs is essential.

topics.title: Other Blood and Tissue Parasites
topics.summary: Trypanosomes, Leishmania, microfilariae and Toxoplasma: specimens and identification.

notes.b: African trypanosomes (T. brucei gambiense in West Africa) are extracellular flagellates with an undulating membrane and small kinetoplast, seen in blood, lymph node aspirates (early stage) and CSF (late stage — also raised CSF white cells > 5/µL); concentration methods (buffy coat, mini-anion exchange centrifugation) improve detection; the CATT serological test screens populations. Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman–Donovan bodies — small oval bodies with a nucleus and rod-shaped kinetoplast inside macrophages) are found in spleen, bone marrow or lymph node aspirates (visceral leishmaniasis) and skin scrapings or biopsies (cutaneous leishmaniasis); promastigotes grow in NNN culture medium.

Microfilariae are identified by size, sheath, nuclear arrangement in the tail and periodicity. Wuchereria bancrofti: sheathed, nuclei do not extend to the tip of the tail, nocturnal periodicity — collect blood between about 10 pm and 2 am. Loa loa: sheathed, nuclei extend to the tail tip, diurnal periodicity — collect around midday. Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae live in skin, not blood — diagnosis by skin snips incubated in saline; unsheathed. Mansonella perstans is unsheathed and common in blood. Concentration techniques: Knott's method, membrane filtration. Toxoplasma gondii infection is usually diagnosed serologically (IgM for recent infection, IgG avidity), with PCR in congenital or ocular cases.
k: Loa loa: sheathed, diurnal, nuclei to tail tip

topics.title: Intestinal Protozoa and Stool Examination
topics.summary: Specimen collection, wet mounts, concentration techniques, and identification of intestinal protozoa.

notes.b: Stool should be collected in a clean, dry, leak-proof container, free of urine and water, and examined fresh — liquid stools within 30 minutes (to see motile trophozoites) and formed stools within a few hours; preservatives (formalin, SAF) are used when delays are expected. Macroscopic examination notes consistency, blood, mucus and adult worms. Microscopy: direct saline wet mount (motile trophozoites, cells, eggs) and iodine wet mount (cyst nuclei and glycogen). Concentration techniques increase sensitivity: formol–ether (formalin–ethyl acetate) sedimentation (the most widely used) and flotation (zinc sulphate or saturated salt — light eggs and cysts float; not suitable for heavy or operculate eggs). Several specimens on different days increase detection. Permanent stains (trichrome) and modified Ziehl–Neelsen (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora oocysts — acid-fast) are used as needed.
k: Saline mount: trophozoites; iodine mount: cysts

notes.b: Entamoeba histolytica: trophozoites with ingested red cells (diagnostic of invasive amoebiasis), cysts with up to 4 nuclei and cigar-shaped chromatoid bars; it is morphologically identical to non-pathogenic E. dispar, so antigen tests or PCR are needed for confirmation. Entamoeba coli (non-pathogenic): cysts with up to 8 nuclei. Giardia lamblia (intestinalis): pear-shaped trophozoites with two nuclei ('face'), falling-leaf motility; oval cysts with four nuclei; causes malabsorptive diarrhoea. Cryptosporidium: small acid-fast oocysts; chronic diarrhoea in AIDS. Balantidium coli is the only ciliate pathogen of humans (from pigs). Trichomonas vaginalis is examined in vaginal or urethral wet mounts (jerky motility).
k: E. histolytica: ingested red cells; 4-nucleate cysts

topics.title: Helminth Eggs and Larvae
topics.summary: Identification of eggs of intestinal nematodes, cestodes and trematodes, and egg counting.

notes.b: Ascaris lumbricoides: fertile eggs are oval with a thick mammillated (bumpy) coat, often bile-stained brown; infertile eggs are longer with irregular coats. Hookworm (Necator, Ancylostoma): thin-shelled, oval, with a segmented embryo (4–8 cell stage) and clear space; in delayed samples eggs may hatch into rhabditiform larvae — confusion with Strongyloides. Trichuris trichiura: barrel- or lemon-shaped with bipolar plugs. Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm): flattened on one side (D-shaped), collected by cellophane (Scotch) tape from the perianal area in the early morning. Strongyloides stercoralis: rhabditiform larvae (not eggs) in fresh stool; Baermann technique or agar plate culture concentrate larvae. The Kato–Katz technique quantifies eggs per gram of stool to assess intensity of infection in surveys.

Taenia species eggs (T. saginata — beef; T. solium — pork) are round with a thick radially striated shell containing a hexacanth (six-hooked) embryo; species are distinguished by gravid proglottids (uterine branches) or molecular tests. Hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm): eggs with polar filaments. Diphyllobothrium: operculate eggs. Schistosoma haematobium: large eggs with a terminal spine, found in terminal urine (collected around midday, after exercise; filtration or sedimentation) — also detect haematuria with dipsticks. S. mansoni: lateral spine, in stool. Fasciola hepatica: large operculate eggs. Hatching tests show viable schistosome eggs. Accurate reporting includes species and, for surveys, egg counts.
k: Taenia: radially striated shell, hexacanth embryo
S. haematobium: terminal spine; midday urine

topics.title: Medical Entomology
topics.summary: Mosquitoes, flies, ticks, lice and mites of medical importance, and principles of vector control.

notes.b: Mosquitoes: Anopheles (malaria, lymphatic filariasis) — adults rest at an angle to the surface; palps as long as the proboscis in both sexes; eggs laid singly with floats; larvae lie parallel to the water surface (no siphon). Aedes (yellow fever, dengue, Zika, chikungunya) — black and white striped, day-biting, breed in containers. Culex (lymphatic filariasis in urban areas, West Nile) — rest parallel to the surface, larvae hang at an angle with a siphon, breed in polluted water. Flies: Simulium blackflies (onchocerciasis — breed in fast-flowing rivers), Glossina tsetse flies (trypanosomiasis), Phlebotomus/Lutzomyia sandflies (leishmaniasis), Chrysops deer flies (Loa loa), and houseflies (Musca — mechanical transmission of diarrhoeal diseases, trachoma). Only female mosquitoes take blood meals.
k: Anopheles: rests at angle; larvae parallel, no siphon
Culex: larvae with siphon; polluted water

notes.b: Ticks transmit relapsing fever (Ornithodoros), Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever and rickettsial infections; lice (Pediculus humanus) transmit epidemic typhus, trench fever and louse-borne relapsing fever; the rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) transmits plague and murine typhus; the scabies mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) causes itchy burrows (treated with permethrin or ivermectin); reduviid (kissing) bugs transmit Chagas disease in the Americas. Vector control: long-lasting insecticidal nets, indoor residual spraying, larviciding and environmental management (removing breeding sites), personal protection (repellents, clothing), and biological control (larvivorous fish, Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis). Insecticide resistance monitoring (WHO tube tests, CDC bottle assays) guides choices; entomological surveillance measures vector density, biting rates and infectivity (entomological inoculation rate).
